## Recap

- Political science theories are usually **causal**
- But establishing causality is extremely difficult
  - **Reverse causation**
  - **Omitted variable bias**
- Today: the problems mount, but we start to consider solutions, too

## How can we know whether being happy *causes* people to live longer?

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
happiness_data <- read.csv("happiness_polity_2018.csv")
ggplot(happiness_data, aes(x = happiness, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", level = F)
```

## The potential outcomes framework

- A system that can hep us understand what causality *is.*
- *What would the value of the dependent variable be for the same unit at different values of the independent variable?*
- *e.g.,* How long would Fred live if he was extremely happy versus only moderately happy?
- **Counterfactual reasoning:** we consider all of Fred's *potential outcomes*
 
## Potential outcomes = parallel universes{style="color:black;font-size:smaller"}

![](parallel_universes.png){fig-align="center"}

## Potential outcomes

- **Hypothetical,** but **real** (???)
- *What would have happened to a particular unit if it received a particular treatment*
  - That is, if the independent variable took on a particular value for that unit
- **Causality:** the difference between potential outcomes within a single unit.
- *e.g.,* if Fred lives longer in the case in which he is happier, then we know that happiness *caused* Fred's longevity.

## We can compare them like this

```{r, echo = F}
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(dplyr)
fred <- rbind(c("Fred", "Lives to 100", "Lives to 85", "Lives to 75"))

kable(fred,
      col.names = c("Unit", "\"very happy\"", "\"pretty happy\"", "\"unhappy\"")) %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Potential outcome if..." = 3))
```

- Effect of being "very happy" instead of "unhappy" = 25 years of extra life!
- Effect of being "very happy" instead of "pretty happy" = 15 years

# But of course, Fred has but one life to live...

## So this is all we can actually observe

```{r, echo = F}
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(dplyr)
fred <- rbind(c("Fred", "???", "Lives to 85", "???"))

kable(fred,
      col.names = c("Unit", "\"very happy\"", "\"pretty happy\"", "\"unhappy\"")) %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Potential outcome if..." = 3))
```

- This is **the fundamental problem of causal inference!**
- We can never observe more than one potential outcome per unit
- Put differently: only one *potential* outcome can ever become a *real* outcome

## So what can we do?

- FPCI $\rightarrow$ we can never directly observe causal relationships at the **individual** level
- BUT we can estimate *average* treatment effects across groups of people!
-  New research question: does a candidate training program increase the likelihood that women will run for office?

::::: r-stack

```{r}
group<- c(rep("Attended training", 3), rep("Did not attend", 3), "")
names <- c("Olivia", "Katie", "Ashlynd", "Camille", "Christina", "Ivy", "Fraction running")
attended <- c("Ran for office", "Ran for office", "Ran for office", "???", "???", "???", "3/3")
didnt <- c("???", "???", "???", "Ran for office", "Did not run", "Did not run", "1/3")
kable(cbind(names, group, attended, didnt),
      col.names = c("Person", "Treatment", "Attended", "Did not attend"),
      align = "cccc") %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "1.5cm") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "1.8cm") %>%
  column_spec(3, color = c("white", "white", "white", "black", "black", "black", "#FFFFFF00"), background = c("green", "green", "green", "#FFFFFF00", "#FFFFFF00", "#FFFFFF00", "#FFFFFF00"), width = "6cm") %>%
  column_spec(4, width = "6cm") %>%
  row_spec(4:7, color = "white") %>%
 collapse_rows(columns = 2, valign = "middle") %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Potential outcomes" = 2)) %>%
  kable_styling(font_size = 28)
```

# So does attending the training *cause* women to run for office?

## What if...

```{r}
group <- c(rep("Attended training", 3), rep("Did not attend", 3))
names <- c("Olivia", "Katie", "Ashlynd", "Camille", "Christina", "Ivy")
attended <- c("Ran for office", "Ran for office", "Ran for office", "Would run", "Would not run", "Would not run")
didnt <- c("Would still run", "Would still run", "Would still run", "Ran for office", "Did not run", "Did not run")
kable(cbind(names, group, attended, didnt),
      col.names = c("Person", "Treatment", "Attended", "Did not attend"),
      align = "cccc") %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "1.5cm") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "1.8cm") %>%
  column_spec(3, color = c("white", "white", "white", "white", "white", "white"), background = c("green", "green", "green", "#8ec080", "grey50", "grey50"), width = "6cm") %>%
  column_spec(4, color = c("white", "white", "white", "white", "white", "white"), background = c("#8ec080", "#8ec080", "#8ec080", "green", "grey20", "grey20"), width = "6cm") %>%
 collapse_rows(columns = 2, valign = "middle") %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Potential outcomes" = 2)) %>%
  kable_styling(font_size = 28)
```

## We have to ask: how was treatment assigned?

- **Selection bias:** some systematic difference influences which units are "treated" and which are not
  - *e.g.,* existing political ambition
- In the language of potential outcomes, treated and untreated units would have different potential outcomes
- A form of **omitted variable bias**

## Codebook

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

codebook <- data.frame(
  Variable = c("name", "participate", "baseline", "po_control", "po_treat"),
  Description = c(
    "Respondent name",
    "0 = did not participate in the wellness program; 1 = did participate",
    "Average monthly medical costs at baseline (before the program started)",
    "Monthly medical cost after the program started <strong>if the person did <em>not</em> participate</strong>",
    "Monthly medical cost after the program started <strong>if the person <em>did</em> participate</strong>"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

kable(codebook, format = "html", escape = FALSE, align = "ll") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, position = "center", font_size = 24) |>
  column_spec(1, monospace = TRUE, bold = TRUE) |>
  column_spec(2, width = "32em")
```

## Takeaways

- Sometimes, individual treatment effects are zero (or the opposite of what we expected!)
- But we can never observe the true treatment effect for any specific individual in real life (FPCI)
- In your groups, you'll analyze a real dataset where only one potential outcome per unit is realized...
